newsitem.title: ITALY: North Korea harvest will not stop famine-UN agency.
newsitem.headline: North Korea harvest will not stop famine-UN agency.

text.p: North Korea's forthcoming harvests will still not yield enough to stop the threat of famine, the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) warned on Tuesday.
"Even under the most optimistic scenario, food this year will fall short of requirements," Ajay Markanday, an economist at the Rome-based agency, told a news conference.
FAO said that although North Korea was unlikely to suffer devastating floods like those in 1995-96, the next harvest in October would fall well short of self-sufficiency levels.

"Overall, production of rice and maize in 1997 is provisionally forecast at about four million tonnes...providing that favourable weather conditions continue and that part of the crop is not consumed prematurely as last year, due to food shortages," the report said.
Markanday said the communist state would still rely on international donor contributions to meet its needs for most of next year unless more long-term farm projects were implemented.
"The situation won't be remedied by the (1998) harvest unless the medium to long term problems are addressed," he said.
One of the major problems was that only 20 percent of overall land in North Korea is suitable for growing crops.
The climate also meant farmers could only plant crops from May to October, Markanday said.
FAO consultant Hans-Peter Mueller, who returned this week from a visit to North Korea, said the agency had implemented double-cropping schemes to make better use of cultivated land.

He added that a recent FAO appeal for fertilisers would also help farmers grow a healthy crop. Emergency food aid would, however, remain crucial to stave off starvation until long-term measures took hold.
"The public distribution system is near collapse," he said. "All food needs are being met by food imports or assistance."
Markanday said the industrial south, which relies heavily on state distribution, was particularly dependent on international food handouts, while the north could barter with China.
The World Food Programme (WFP), the Rome-based U.N. food aid agency, launched a $46 million appeal last week to feed children in its latest attempt to help the near-starving population.

Washington quickly pledged $27 million, bringing its 1997 contributions to $57 million in what was regarded as a goodwill gesture ahead of peace talks between North Korea, South Korea, China and the United States due to start in New York on August 5.
